title: The anatomy of persuasion
objectives: Distinguish credibility, emotion, and reasoning.
State what you want an audience to think or do.
lesson: An appeal is a route to persuasion, not proof by itself. Credibility makes a speaker easier to trust; reasons still need checking.
Start with an audience need. Explain one concrete consequence, then connect evidence to your claim.
practice: Write one claim in three versions: credibility-led, emotion-led, and evidence-led.
Deliver a 60-second introduction. Ask a listener to repeat your central point.
assessment: A 90-second speech using all three appeals without inventing evidence.

title: Build an argument that holds
objectives: Separate grounds from warrants.
Qualify a claim and name an exception.
lesson: Grounds are what you offer as support; the warrant explains why those grounds justify your claim. A missing warrant is a common source of disagreement.
Add backing for a disputed warrant. Use a qualifier such as usually or under these conditions, and state a real rebuttal condition.
practice: Map a real opinion into all six Toulmin elements.
Ask a partner to challenge your warrant, then revise it.
assessment: One six-part argument with a clearly stated limitation.

title: Spot the broken inference
objectives: Identify a flaw in the inference, not just a label.
Distinguish a weak argument from a false conclusion.
lesson: A fallacious argument can happen to reach a true conclusion. Diagnose how the offered support fails.
For each label, write a plain-language explanation. Then repair the argument by adding evidence or narrowing its scope.
practice: Complete five Fallacy Spotter rounds.
Rewrite three flawed claims so the evidence matches their scope.
assessment: Five diagnoses with reasons and repaired claims.

title: Make structure second nature
readingFocus: Testing the support behind a conclusion
objectives: Give a direct answer before elaborating.
Combine a clear structure with valid reasoning.
lesson: PREP moves from Point to Reason to Example and back to Point. An example illustrates a reason but may not establish a general rule.
Use your final point to state what follows and what remains uncertain. Brevity should expose your logic, not hide its gaps.
practice: Answer six everyday prompts in 60 seconds each.
Review one recording for claim clarity, support, and unsupported generalizations.
assessment: A two-minute argument and a written self-review.

title: Understand before opposing
objectives: Present an opposing view in terms its holder could accept.
Separate the strongest claim from an easy target.
lesson: Before criticizing a view, identify its best evidence and its most reasonable scope. Do not turn a modest proposal into an extreme one.
Steel-manning is a charitable reconstruction, not agreement. Ask whether your opponent recognizes the restatement.
practice: Write the strongest case for a view you oppose.
Answer that case without commenting on the speaker’s character.
assessment: A fair 90-second opposing case and a focused response.

title: Concede with precision
readingFocus: Agreement as an opening for persuasion
objectives: Concede a true point without overstating its implications.
Distinguish values, facts, and policy choices.
lesson: A limited concession can make the remaining disagreement clearer. State exactly what the evidence establishes.
Agreeing that a problem is serious does not commit you to every proposed solution. Compare alternatives against shared criteria.
practice: Practice six concession phrases from the phrasebook.
Write three responses that accept a premise but test the conclusion.
assessment: A response containing a concession, a boundary, and a reasoned alternative.

title: Find the load-bearing premise
objectives: Identify a premise the conclusion depends on.
Ask for the evidence that could test it.
lesson: A load-bearing premise is one whose failure would weaken the conclusion. Check it before debating secondary details.
For causal claims, consider sequence, plausible mechanisms, comparison groups, and alternative explanations. Correlation alone leaves work to do.
practice: Underline the hidden warrant in four arguments.
Formulate one discriminating question for each.
assessment: Four premise maps and four questions that could change the conclusion.

title: Respond without losing the thread
objectives: Refute the actual claim with a specific reason.
Return to the question after a diversion.
lesson: Use four moves: they say, I respond, because, therefore. Each move has a job; keep the implication tied to the objection.
When a new topic appears, determine whether it matters to the original claim. Acknowledge it and return to the unresolved inference when needed.
practice: Complete six timed refutations.
Redo the weakest one with a narrower objection and a better counterexample.
assessment: A three-minute rebuttal that addresses two real objections.

title: Choose the frame deliberately
readingFocus: How presentation shapes an audience’s attention
objectives: Distinguish description from evaluation.
Make a frame explicit and test what it omits.
lesson: A frame foregrounds some aspects of a choice. Calling a measure an investment or a cost directs attention differently without settling its value.
Replace a loaded word with a neutral description, then ask which facts remain. Keep comparisons consistent across options.
practice: Describe the same policy through cost, fairness, and opportunity frames.
Identify one important consideration each frame leaves out.
assessment: Three frames and a neutral statement of the underlying facts.

title: Build a vocabulary you can use
objectives: Decode unfamiliar words using roots and affixes.
Use new vocabulary in a natural spoken sentence.
lesson: Roots and affixes are clues, not guarantees: historical meanings and modern usage can differ. Verify the full word and its register.
A word becomes useful through retrieval in context. Explain it simply, say it aloud, and use it while answering a question.
practice: Learn eight lexicon words and review due cards daily.
Deliver a one-minute answer using three of those words naturally.
assessment: Eight word explanations and two spoken responses.

title: Give ideas a rhythm
objectives: Use pauses at idea boundaries.
Build parallel phrases without obscuring meaning.
lesson: Cadence comes from stress, sentence length, and silence. Mark the main thought before you mark where to breathe.
Parallel clauses make relationships audible. Keep the grammar aligned and avoid a flourish that overstates your evidence.
practice: Mark pauses in a 150-word speech.
Record the same passage at two speeds and compare intelligibility.
assessment: A 90-second delivery with intentional pauses and one three-part cadence.

title: Stay precise under pressure
objectives: Match tone to purpose and relationship.
Use specific vocabulary without sounding forced.
lesson: A measured tone can preserve cooperation during disagreement. A decisive tone can make a conclusion clear once the reasoning is established.
Under time pressure, prefer a familiar accurate word to an impressive uncertain one. Self-correct promptly if a word does not fit.
practice: Complete tone-matching and speed-recall drills.
Answer three challenges, using a different tone for each.
assessment: Three two-minute defenses using at least three target words each.

title: Ask the question that matters
objectives: Ask one question at a time.
Test a claim without smuggling in a disputed premise.
lesson: A useful question reduces uncertainty: what exactly is claimed, what supports it, and what would count against it?
Avoid a loaded question that assumes what you are trying to prove. Listen to the answer and adjust the next question accordingly.
practice: Write a sequence of five short, neutral questions.
Practice responding to an ambiguous question by requesting clarification.
assessment: A five-minute cross-examination with a fair summary of the answers.

title: Think on your feet
objectives: Choose a structure quickly.
Separate a useful example from an unverified fact.
lesson: Use preparation time to choose a point and a structure. A short, defensible claim is easier to develop than an ambitious vague one.
Label hypothetical examples. If you do not know a fact, explain what information you would need instead of manufacturing a statistic.
practice: Take eight random prompts with 20 seconds of preparation.
Speak for 90 seconds using PREP and one concession.
assessment: Four recorded responses with clear reasoning and no invented evidence.

title: Close the case
readingFocus: Comparing the strength of competing arguments
objectives: Weigh competing reasons against shared criteria.
End with a proportionate request or conclusion.
lesson: A closing identifies the decisive issue and explains why one option better meets the agreed criteria. It does not merely repeat every point.
Address the strongest remaining objection and state residual uncertainty. End with a concrete conclusion matched to the evidence.
practice: Reduce a debate to three issues and rank their importance.
Deliver a two-minute closing that includes the strongest objection.
assessment: A closing with explicit weighing, a concession, and a concrete recommendation.

title: Your final pressure test
objectives: Integrate structure, refutation, vocabulary, and delivery.
Name what would change your mind.
lesson: Run a full round: opening, questions, rebuttal, and closing. Keep track of which claims are established and which are still disputed.
Evaluate accuracy, charity, structure, and delivery separately. The goal is a defensible position communicated clearly, including correction when warranted.
practice: Complete a 12-minute mock debate and a final vocabulary review.
Compare with your week-one speech and write a maintenance plan.
assessment: A complete debate, a rubric-based review, and a 30-day continuation plan.
